hints: Think about what happens when a $\text{-COCl}$ group meets a $\text{-NH}_2$ group, what small molecule is lost and what link remains.
Keep the substitution patterns of the two benzene rings unchanged, 1,4 for the diacid part and 1,3 for the diamine part, and extend the chain to show continuation.
walkthrough:
Spot the reacting groups**
You have $\text{-C(=O)Cl}$ on one monomer and $\text{H}_2\text{N-}$ on the other. When they meet, $\text{Cl}$ from the acyl chloride and $\text{H}$ from the amine leave together as $\text{HCl}$. What is left behind is a $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ amide link. That is the only new bond you need to make.

Keep the rings exactly as given**
Do not redraw the benzene rings in new positions. The left monomer stays para, 1,4, so the two $\text{C=O}$ groups are opposite each other. The right monomer stays meta, 1,3, so the two $\text{NH}$ groups are one carbon apart. Draw two of each ring alternating: diacid ring, amide, diamine ring, amide, diacid ring, amide, diamine ring, amide.

Show it is a polymer**
A section with two repeat units means four rings in total in the order shown above. Finish with a short bond sticking out at the left end and at the right end to show the chain continues. Those trailing bonds tell the reader this is part of a much longer chain.

Final answer: Section showing alternating units: $\text{-CO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO-NH-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NH-}$ repeated twice, with 1,4-disubstitution on the diacyl ring and 1,3-disubstitution on the diamine ring, all $\text{-CO-NH-}$ amide links correct, and trailing bonds at both ends.

hints: Look at the link you just formed in (i) and recall whether $\text{-CONH-}$ belongs to a polyamide or a polyester.
walkthrough:
Link the name to the link**
The repeating link is $\text{-CO-NH-}$, the amide group. A chain held together by amide links is a polyamide. Because each link forms with loss of a small molecule, $\text{HCl}$, this is condensation polymerisation, not addition.
Final answer: Tick polyamide and condensation.

hints: Recall the key difference between addition C-C chains and condensation chains when water or enzymes attack.
walkthrough:
Connect hydrolysis to breakdown**
Condensation links can be split again by the reverse reaction. Water can add across the $\text{-CO-NH-}$ bond to give back carboxylic acid and amine. Because microorganisms and enzymes can catalyse this hydrolysis, the chain can be broken into small molecules, so polymer P counts as biodegradable.
Final answer: Yes, biodegradable because amide links can be hydrolysed by water, acids or enzymes.

hints: Think of the standard reagents that replace $\text{-OH}$ of a $\text{-COOH}$ group by $\text{-Cl}$.
walkthrough:
Choose the chlorinating agent**
Changing benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COOH})_2$, to benzene-1,4-dioyl chloride, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COCl})_2$, needs $\text{OH}$ replaced by $\text{Cl}$. Any of thionyl chloride, $\text{SOCl}_2$, phosphorus(V) chloride, $\text{PCl}_5$, or phosphorus(III) chloride, $\text{PCl}_3$, does this cleanly.
Final answer: $\text{SOCl}_2$ or $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{PCl}_3$.

hints: Identify the type of change in step 1, benzene to nitrobenzene, and recall the pair of acids that generates the nitrating electrophile.
Identify the type of change in step 3, $\text{-NO}_2$ to $\text{-NH}_2$, and recall the metal plus acid reducing mixture used for this.
walkthrough:
Nitrate benzene in step 1**
Benzene to nitrobenzene is electrophilic substitution by $\text{NO}_2^+$. The electrophile is made in situ from concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid: $$\text{HNO}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NO}_2^+ + 2\text{HSO}_4^- + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$$ Heat to about $50$ degrees C. Step 2 then adds the second nitro group in the meta position.

Reduce both nitro groups in step 3**
Changing $\text{O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NO}_2$ to $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NH}_2$ is a 12 electron reduction, $\text{-NO}_2$ to $\text{-NH}_2$. Use tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, $\text{Sn}$ + $\text{HCl}$, with heating, which gives the diammonium salt first. Adding alkali then releases the free diamine.
Final answer: step 1: conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heated; step 3: $\text{Sn}$ + conc. $\text{HCl}$, heated, followed by $\text{NaOH}$ to liberate free amine.

hints: Start from the building blocks, amino acid residues joined in a chain, and think what primary tells you about their arrangement.
Think about local coiling or folding of that chain stabilised by regular hydrogen bonding.
Think about the overall three dimensional folding of the whole chain, including interactions between distant side chains.
walkthrough:
Picture primary as the code**
Imagine beads on a string where each bead is a different amino acid. Primary structure is simply the exact order those amino acids are linked together by peptide bonds, for example gly-ala-ser. Change one bead and the whole protein behaviour can change.

Picture secondary as local shape**
Now let short sections of that string coil or pleat. Hydrogen bonds between backbone $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$ groups pull the chain into a regular $\alpha$-helix, like a spiral staircase, or a $\beta$-pleated sheet, like a folded fan. This is still only local structure.

Picture tertiary as global folding**
Finally the whole helix and sheet regions fold up together into one compact 3-D shape. Side chain interactions such as hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges and hydrophobic interactions hold this overall folding in place. That unique 3-D shape allows enzymes and antibodies to work.

Final answer: primary: sequence or order of amino acids in the polypeptide chain; secondary: coiling into $\alpha$-helix or folding into $\beta$-pleated sheet; tertiary: further folding of chain to give overall 3-D shape of protein.

hints: Recall what strong bond links one amino acid to the next in the backbone and whether it can be broken without chemical reaction.
walkthrough:
Name the backbone bond**
Amino acids join by condensation between $\text{-COOH}$ and $\text{-NH}_2$ to give $\text{-CO-NH-}$. This is a covalent peptide bond, also called an amide bond. It is strong and defines the primary sequence.
Final answer: Covalent bonds, peptide (amide) bonds.

hints: Recall the weak interaction that stabilises alpha helices and beta sheets rather than the strong covalent backbone.
Identify which polar groups on the polypeptide backbone act as donor and acceptor for that interaction.
walkthrough:
Identify the stabilising force**
Secondary structure is not held by new covalent bonds. It is held by many weak hydrogen bonds acting together along the backbone. Individually weak, collectively they lock the helix or sheet in place.

Pinpoint the groups involved**
The carbonyl oxygen, $\text{C=O}$, is electron rich and acts as the hydrogen bond acceptor. The amide hydrogen, $\text{N-H}$, acts as the donor: $$\text{C=O} \cdots \text{H-N}$$ This regular $\text{C=O} \cdots \text{H-N}$ bonding between different parts of the chain stabilises the $\alpha$-helix and $\beta$-sheet.
Final answer: Hydrogen bonds between $\text{C=O}$ of one peptide group and $\text{N-H}$ of another peptide group.
